title: Google File System

definition.text: A proprietary distributed file system that Google built to give efficient, reliable access to data on large clusters of commodity hardware.

facts.text: GFS was built for Google's core storage needs, mainly the search engine, which generates enormous amounts of data that must be retained.
It runs on clusters of cheap commodity computers, so it must guard against the high failure rate of individual nodes and the data loss that follows.
Files are split into fixed-size chunks of 64 megabytes; they are usually appended to or read, and only extremely rarely overwritten or shrunk.
Other design decisions favor high data throughput even when it costs latency.
A cluster has one master node and many chunkservers; the master gives each chunk a globally unique 64-bit label when it creates it and keeps the mapping from files to chunks.
Each chunk is replicated across the network, three times by default but configurable; files in high demand may get a higher replication factor.
The master stores metadata rather than chunks, including where each chunk's copies live, and stays current through periodic heartbeat messages from every chunkserver.
Modifications are controlled by time-limited leases: the master lets one process modify a chunk for a finite period, and no other process gets permission during it.
The primary chunk holder pushes each change to the backup chunkservers, and the change is not saved until all of them acknowledge, which makes the operation atomic.
A client asks the master where a chunk lives, then reads the data directly from a chunkserver, so the master stays out of the data path.
Record Append lets many clients append to the same file at once, with atomicity guaranteed; GFS does not provide a POSIX interface.
Because the master is not involved in reads, read rate grows with the number of chunkservers, reaching 583 MB/s for 342 nodes.

title: Spanner

definition.text: Google's scalable, multiversion, globally distributed and synchronously replicated SQL database.

facts.text: It offers global transactions, strongly consistent reads, and automatic multi-site replication and failover.
Its authors describe it as the first system to distribute data at global scale and support externally-consistent distributed transactions.
Users can run arbitrary SQL queries on relational data while keeping strong consistency and high availability through synchronous replication.
Transactions can span rows, columns, tables and databases within one Spanner universe.
Reads are strongly consistent and data is versioned, so clients can read previous versions of data, subject to garbage collection windows.
Spanner uses the Paxos algorithm to shard data across up to hundreds of servers, with data spread over many Paxos state machines.
It leans on hardware-assisted clock synchronization with GPS and atomic clocks, and its TrueTime service gives it monotonically increasing timestamps in data centers worldwide.
The paper's time API exposes clock uncertainty and is critical to external consistency, nonblocking reads in the past, lock-free snapshot transactions and atomic schema changes.

notes: Wikipedia's sentence calling TrueTime 'the brand name for Google's distributed cloud infrastructure' is loose; the paper abstract is the better description of the time API.

title: Amazon DynamoDB

definition.text: A managed NoSQL database service from AWS that supports key-value and document data and is built for scalability and performance.

facts.text: Many Amazon services mostly read by primary key and put speed first, so Amazon built Dynamo, a highly available key-value store, and accepted lower storage efficiency.
Engineers avoided Dynamo because of the overhead of provisioning and managing partitions and nodes; DynamoDB automated those operations.
Data lives in tables of items made of attributes, and a table does not require its items to follow a predefined schema.
DynamoDB hashes the partition key to pick a partition; each partition stores up to 10 GB and by default handles 1,000 write capacity units and 3,000 read capacity units.
One read capacity unit is one strongly consistent read per second, or two eventually consistent reads, for items up to 4 KB; one write capacity unit is one write per second for an item up to 1 KB.
Each partition has three nodes holding copies, with one leader chosen by Paxos; the leader sends a heartbeat every 1.5 seconds, and a node that stops hearing it can start a new election.
A write goes to the leader, then a second node, then returns success while propagation continues to the third node; writes stay consistent because they always pass through the leader.
A consistent read visits the leader, while an eventually consistent read picks a random node, trading consistency for availability so reads do not overload one node.

title: DynamoDB partition and sort keys
article: Amazon DynamoDB#Overview > DynamoDB Items > Keys In DynamoDB

definition.text: The primary key of a DynamoDB table is one or two attributes that uniquely identify each item and decide where it is stored.

facts.text: Creating a table requires a primary key, every item must carry all its key attributes, and no two items in a table can share a primary key.
A primary key of one attribute is a partition key, which determines the physical location of the item; no two items can have the same partition key.

A primary key of two attributes is a partition key plus a sort key: the partition key picks the physical location, the sort key orders items inside it, and items may share a partition key but not a sort key.
A local secondary index keeps the table's partition key with a different sort key; a global secondary index uses a different partition key.

title: DynamoDB data modeling patterns
article: Amazon DynamoDB#Architectural patterns in DynamoDB data modeling

definition.text: A set of ways to lay out data in DynamoDB, chosen to match a workload's access patterns.

facts.text: Single Table Design keeps related data together under one partition key, within the 400KB item size limit, to cut access latency.
Multiple Table Design isolates data into purpose-specific tables by access pattern, and Hybrid Design blends the two approaches.
Event Sourcing stores data changes as immutable events so past state can be rebuilt, and Materialized Views pre-aggregate data, often via DynamoDB Streams or Lambda batch updates.
Time-Series Design suits logging and metrics: the partition key identifies the entity and the sort key holds the timestamp.

definition.text: Discord moved its message storage from MongoDB to Cassandra to ScyllaDB as its data grew to trillions of messages.

facts.text: Discord's first version stored messages on a single MongoDB replica.
Around Nov 2015 MongoDB held 100 million messages and RAM could no longer hold the data and index, so latency became unpredictable and storage had to move.
Cassandra was chosen: in 2017 Discord ran 12 Cassandra nodes with billions of messages, and at the start of 2022 it ran 177 nodes with trillions.
By then Cassandra latency was unpredictable and maintenance operations had become too expensive to run.
Cassandra's LSM tree makes reads more expensive than writes, and many concurrent reads on a server with hundreds of users create hotspots.
Cluster maintenance such as compacting SSTables hurts performance, and garbage collection pauses cause significant latency spikes.
ScyllaDB is a Cassandra-compatible database written in C++.
Discord redesigned its architecture around a monolithic API, a data service written in Rust, and ScyllaDB-based storage.
The p99 read latency is 15ms on ScyllaDB against 40-125ms on Cassandra; the p99 write latency is 5ms against 5-70ms.

definition.text: An open-source distributed database that handles very large amounts of data across many commodity servers with no single point of failure.

facts.text: Cassandra was designed to run on cheap commodity hardware and handle high write throughput without sacrificing read efficiency.
It aims to run on hundreds of nodes, possibly across data centers, where components fail continuously, so how it manages persistent state under failure drives its reliability and scalability.
It combines Amazon's Dynamo storage and replication techniques with Google's Bigtable data storage engine model to give all clients low-latency operations.
All nodes perform identical functions, so there is no single point of failure; replication is asynchronous and masterless, and a cluster can span multiple data centers.
It scales linearly: adding nodes raises read and write throughput while service continues.
Cassandra is classed as an AP system, favoring availability and partition tolerance over consistency; consistency levels are tunable for reads and writes, but strict consistency suits it poorly.
It does not support a full relational model: it offers a simple wide-column model with dynamic control over layout, and suits well-defined access patterns that can be built into the schema.
It does not support multi-table JOINs, ad hoc aggregations or complex queries, because its distributed architecture optimizes for scalability and availability instead.

definition.text: Cassandra stores data in keyspaces of tables whose rows are found by a partition key and may each have different columns.

facts.text: Data is organized as keyspace, table, then row; a keyspace is like a database and defines the replication strategy, so replication is set at the keyspace level.
Each row is identified by a primary key whose first component is the partition key; within a partition, rows are clustered by the remaining key columns.
Rows in one table can have different columns, and tables can be created, dropped or altered at run-time without blocking updates and queries.
Each column carries timestamp metadata used to resolve write conflicts by last write wins, and the data model is denormalized rather than joined.

definition.text: Cassandra writes append to a commit log and an in-memory Memtable, which later flushes to immutable SSTables.

facts.text: Cassandra uses a log-structured merge tree index to optimize write throughput, unlike the B-tree indexes most databases use.
A write goes to the commit log, a write-ahead log that ensures durability, and to the Memtable, an in-memory structure sorted by primary key.
When the Memtable reaches size or time thresholds it flushes to an SSTable, an immutable file; reads check the Memtable, then search SSTables from newest to oldest using bloom filters.
Every change adds a new entry and deletes use tombstones, which can slow delete-heavy workloads; compaction merges SSTables to cut storage, drop tombstoned rows and speed reads.

definition.text: Cassandra nodes spread cluster state by peer-to-peer gossip and each node detects failed peers on its own.

facts.text: Nodes routinely gossip cluster state, such as node bootstrap times and logical clock values, and use the clock values to ignore outdated state.
A few seed nodes are guaranteed gossip contact points, which removes single points of failure while keeping cluster-wide knowledge consistent.
Each node judges the availability of others with the Phi Accrual Failure Detector; a node that fails to respond is convicted and removed from writes, but can rejoin when heartbeats resume.
With hinted handoff, the coordinator stores a write meant for an offline node as a hint and forwards it when the node returns; nodes leave permanently only by explicit decommissioning or rebuilding.

definition.text: A collection of open-source software utilities for reliable, scalable, distributed computing, built around HDFS storage and MapReduce processing.

facts.text: Hadoop's core is a storage part, the Hadoop Distributed File System, and a processing part that implements the MapReduce programming model.
Hadoop splits files into large blocks spread across the cluster, then ships packaged code to the nodes so they process in parallel the data they hold, which is data locality.
This lets a dataset be processed faster and more efficiently than on a conventional supercomputer architecture that moves data over high-speed networking from a parallel file system.
The base framework has Hadoop Common, HDFS, YARN (introduced in 2012) for cluster resources and scheduling, and MapReduce; Hadoop Ozone, an object store, came in 2020.
Hadoop's MapReduce and HDFS components were inspired by Google's papers on MapReduce and the Google File System.
Hadoop could in theory serve any batch-oriented, very data-intensive workload that benefits from parallel processing; it is not for real-time work but can complement real-time systems.
Hadoop 3 allows multiple name nodes, which removes the single point of failure of Hadoop 2's one namenode, and uses erasure coding to decrease storage overhead.
Yahoo's Search Webmap, a Hadoop application on a Linux cluster of more than 10,000 cores, produced data used in every Yahoo! web search query.

title: HDFS architecture
article: Apache Hadoop#Architecture > File systems > Hadoop distributed file system

definition.text: HDFS is Hadoop's distributed, scalable file system that stores large files across many machines, with one NameNode tracking metadata and many DataNodes storing blocks.

facts.text: The NameNode tracks files and holds metadata: the number of blocks, which DataNodes store them and where replicas live; it talks directly to clients, while DataNodes store the blocks.
HDFS gets reliability by replicating data across hosts, so it theoretically needs no RAID; with the default replication value 3, two copies sit on one rack and one on a different rack.
Rack-aware replication keeps data available if a rack loses power or a switch fails.
Each DataNode sends a heartbeat to the NameNode every 3 seconds; after 2 minutes without one, the NameNode treats the node as dead and starts replicating its blocks onto other DataNodes.
The secondary namenode is not a failover backup: it checkpoints the primary's directory information so a failed primary can restart without replaying the whole journal of file-system actions.
The single NameNode holds all metadata and can become a bottleneck with many small files; HDFS Federation allows multiple namespaces served by separate namenodes.
HDFS gives up full POSIX compliance for higher data throughput and non-POSIX operations such as Append, and it suits mostly immutable files rather than concurrent writes.

title: Hadoop job scheduling and YARN
article: Apache Hadoop#Architecture > JobTracker and TaskTracker: the MapReduce engine

definition.text: In first-generation Hadoop a JobTracker hands MapReduce work to TaskTrackers close to the data, and YARN later replaced this engine.

facts.text: Clients submit MapReduce jobs to one JobTracker, which pushes work to available TaskTracker nodes and tries to keep work as close to the data as possible.

With a rack-aware file system, work that cannot run on the node holding the data goes to a node in the same rack, which reduces traffic on the main backbone network; a failed TaskTracker's work is rescheduled.
Hadoop schedules by FIFO with 5 priorities by default; the fair scheduler gives pools a guaranteed minimum share, and the capacity scheduler gives queues a fraction of total capacity.
YARN, the biggest change in Hadoop 2, replaced the MapReduce engine: a resource manager does job tracking and resource allocation, and an application master monitors execution of each application.

definition.text: A distributed storage system for structured data designed to scale to petabytes of data across thousands of commodity servers.

facts.text: Many Google projects store data in Bigtable, such as web indexing, Google Earth and Google Finance, with demands from URLs to satellite imagery in size and from bulk processing to real-time serving in latency.
Google's reasons for building its own database include scalability and better control of performance characteristics.
Bigtable scales to the petabyte range across hundreds or thousands of machines, and added machines are used automatically without any reconfiguration.
It is built on Colossus (Google File System), the Chubby Lock Service and SSTable log-structured storage.
Tables are split into tablets of a few hundred megabytes or a few gigabytes, and thousands to hundreds of thousands of tablets are served by hundreds to thousands of Bigtable servers.
Tablet locations live in META1 tablets, found via the single META0 tablet; it is not a bottleneck because lookups are cheap and clients aggressively cache locations.
Apache HBase and Cassandra are the best-known open source projects modeled after Bigtable.
As of April 2024, Bigtable manages over 10 Exabytes of data and serves more than 7 billion requests per second.

definition.text: Bigtable is a sparse, distributed, multi-dimensional sorted map that maps a row key, a column key and a timestamp to a byte array.

facts.text: It maps two arbitrary strings, a row key and a column key, plus a timestamp, a three-dimensional mapping, to an arbitrary byte array.
It is not a relational database, is a prototypical wide-column store, and gives clients dynamic control over data layout and format.
Each cell can hold zero or more timestamped versions of its data, and timestamps allow both versioning and garbage collection of expired data.
Google's copy of the web fits one table: the row key is a domain-reversed URL, columns describe page properties, and the page column keeps versions stamped by fetch time.

definition.text: A programming model and implementation for processing large data sets on a cluster: the user writes a map function and a reduce function, and the runtime parallelizes the work.

facts.text: Users write a map function, which filters and sorts, and a reduce function, which summarizes; the runtime parallelizes the work across the cluster, handles machine failures and schedules communication to use the network and disks efficiently.
Its key contribution is not the map and reduce functions but the scalability and fault tolerance it gives a variety of applications through parallelization.
Map has each worker apply the map function to its local data; shuffle redistributes data by output key so one key's data sits on one worker; reduce processes each key's group in parallel.
It processes data near where it is stored to cut communication overhead, and a large server farm can use it to sort a petabyte of data in only a few hours.

Workers report back periodically; if a node falls silent, the master marks it dead and gives its work to other nodes, and a failed mapper or reducer can be rescheduled while the input data remains available.

The paper reports more than ten thousand distinct MapReduce programs at Google over four years, and an average of one hundred thousand jobs a day processing more than twenty petabytes of data per day.

It is usually not effective for quick jobs whose data fits in the memory of one machine, because writing interim results to distributed storage for crash recovery only pays off with many computers and long runtimes.
Tasks must be acyclic dataflow programs, a stateless mapper then a stateless reducer, which makes iterative algorithms such as graph processing difficult.

definition.text: A MapReduce job flows through an input reader, map, partition, shuffle, sort, reduce and output writer.

facts.text: The input reader cuts input from stable storage, typically a distributed file system, into splits of typically 64 MB to 128 MB, one per Map call; map turns each key/value pair into zero or more output pairs.
A partition function sends each map output to a reducer, typically by hashing the key modulo the number of reducers; it should spread data roughly uniformly, or the job waits on slow reducers.
Between map and reduce the data is shuffled across nodes, which can take longer than the computation itself; a Combiner function can reduce the data written to disk and sent over the network.
The framework calls Reduce once per unique key in sorted order; in word count, map emits each word with a count and reduce sums them, and the output writer saves the result to stable storage.

title: Amazon Dynamo

definition.text: Amazon's highly available key-value store, built for internal use to keep persistent state reliable while components fail all the time.

facts.text: Reliability at massive scale is one of Amazon's biggest challenges, because even the slightest outage has significant financial consequences and impacts customer trust.
The Amazon.com platform runs on tens of thousands of servers and network components in many datacenters around the world.
At that scale, small and large components fail continuously, and how persistent state is managed in the face of these failures drives the reliability and scalability of the software.
Many Amazon services mostly read data by primary key and put speed first; joining the pieces of data that traditional databases split apart was extremely taxing.
Amazon's response was Dynamo, a highly available key-value store built for internal use, which accepted a compromise in storage efficiency.
Adoption lagged because engineers avoided the overhead of provisioning and managing partitions and nodes; the later DynamoDB service automated those operations.
Cassandra incorporates Dynamo's distributed storage and replication techniques.
